title: Psalm 109: A Prayer Against the Accuser
summary: A man falsely accused by people he had loved cries to God not to stay silent. A long series of curses against an enemy follows, asking that his life be short, his family ruined, and his name erased. The psalmist then describes his own weakness and poverty, asks God to save him by his loving devotion, and ends by praising the God who stands at the right hand of the needy.
story: Psalm 109 is the second of three psalms of David (108 to 110) placed early in Book V. Psalm 108 asked God for victory over enemy nations; this psalm narrows the conflict to one person accused in court by people close to him. The next psalm, 110, pictures the king seated at God's right hand. Read in order, the three move from national danger, to the personal suffering of a righteous man, to the enthronement of God's chosen king. Psalm 109 is one of the fiercest of the so-called imprecatory psalms, the psalms that call down judgment on enemies, and it is the one the New Testament uses when it speaks of the betrayal of Jesus.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.” Nothing in the psalm ties it to a particular event in David's life, though the story of his flight from Absalom and the treachery of his counselor Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15 to 17) has often been suggested as the kind of betrayal the psalm describes. Many scholars see the setting as a lawsuit. The language is legal throughout: an accuser stands at the right hand, a man is tried and found guilty, and in the last verse God stands at the right hand of the needy to save him from those who condemn him. Some have proposed that the psalm was prayed at the temple by a person awaiting a verdict. As with most psalm headings, scholars differ on whether “of David” names the author or places the psalm in a Davidic collection.

A long-standing question concerns who speaks the curses in verses 6 to 19. In verses 1 to 5 the enemies are plural; in verses 6 to 19 the curses fall on a single “him”; in verse 20 the plural returns. Some interpreters, and some modern translations, read verses 6 to 19 as the enemies' curse against the psalmist, which he quotes before asking God to overturn it. Others read them as the psalmist's own prayer against the chief accuser, noting that verse 20 seems to ask that exactly this be the LORD's reward to his accusers. The Hebrew allows both readings, and both have careful defenders.
cultural:
In ancient Israel a trial took place at the city gate before elders, and the accuser stood beside the accused. The Hebrew word for accuser in verse 6 is satan, the same word used of the adversary who stands at the right hand of the high priest Joshua to accuse him in Zechariah 3:1. Here it is an ordinary human prosecutor. False witness was a grave crime, and the law of Moses required that a false witness receive the penalty he had tried to bring on another (Deuteronomy 19:16-19). The curses of the psalm follow that logic of measure for measure: the man loved cursing, so let cursing come to him.

The curses reach the family because in that world a man's life continued in his children and his name. To have one's line cut off and name blotted out was to disappear from the community's memory. The creditor seizing everything, children begging among ruins, and no one showing kindness to orphans describe total social collapse. The pictures of clothing (a coat, a robe, a belt) and of water and oil soaking into the body say that the curse should become part of him, the way he made cursing part of himself.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament, the most common type in the Psalter, with a complaint, a petition, and a vow of praise. It has three movements. Verses 1 to 5 state the complaint: lying mouths answer love with hatred. Verses 6 to 20 form the long curse, built on repeated “may” clauses and on the reversal of what the enemy did. Verses 21 to 31 turn with a strong “But You, O GOD, the Lord,” to the psalmist's weakness and God's help. The poem is held together by contrasts: cursing and blessing (verse 28), the accuser at the right hand (verse 6) and God at the right hand (verse 31), the enemy clothed with cursing and the accusers clothed with shame. Verse 4 contains a striking phrase that reads literally but I, prayer, as if the psalmist has become nothing but prayer.

outline.t: Love repaid with lies and hatred
The curse on the accuser and his house
The one who loved cursing receives it
Save me, so they will know it is your hand
Praise for the God at the right hand of the needy

doctrines.note: The psalm asks God, not the psalmist, to judge. Vengeance is handed over rather than taken, which is the same instinct Paul teaches when he says to leave room for God's wrath (Romans 12:19). The prayer is for justice against one who crushed the poor to death.

The psalm shows that rage and grief can be brought to God in words. Scripture does not require the wounded to pray politely; it gives them language for anger and then leads that anger toward God's loving devotion and praise.

The psalmist is poor, fasting, fading like a shadow, and mocked. His suffering is not punishment for his own wrong but the result of others' lies, and God is presented as the one who takes the side of the needy.

words.note: Satan, adversary or accuser. In verse 6 it is a human accuser in court. The related verb (H7853) appears in verses 4, 20, and 29 for the psalmist's accusers. The word later becomes the name of the devil, but here it keeps its basic legal meaning of one who opposes and accuses.

Tefillah, prayer. In verse 4 the Hebrew reads literally but I, prayer, which the BSB renders “but I am a man of prayer.” The phrase answers accusation not with counter-accusation but with prayer, and in verse 7 the psalmist asks that the enemy's own prayer be counted as sin.

Chesed, loyal love or loving devotion. The enemy “never thought to show kindness” (verse 16), and the curse asks that no one show kindness to him (verse 12). The psalmist, by contrast, appeals twice to God's chesed (verses 21 and 26). The word shows the moral center of the psalm: the one who refused kindness is set against the God whose kindness is the psalmist's only hope.

Evyon, needy or poor. The enemy pursued “the poor and needy” (verse 16); the psalmist confesses “I am poor and needy” (verse 22); and God stands “at the right hand of the needy one” (verse 31). The word ties the psalm's anger to the protection of the vulnerable.

christ: When the apostles chose a replacement for Judas, Peter quoted this psalm together with Psalm 69, applying verse 8 to Judas: may another take his position (Acts 1:20). The early church heard in Psalm 109 the voice of the righteous sufferer betrayed by a friend, a pattern that reached its fullest form in Jesus, who was repaid evil for good and whose accusers shook their heads at him (compare verse 25 with Matthew 27:39). Yet Jesus also changes how the psalm is prayed. He taught his followers to bless those who curse them (Luke 6:28), and from the cross he prayed for those who crucified him. Christians have therefore read the curses as a cry for God's justice that Jesus both answers and absorbs: the judgment on sin falls on him, and the God who stands at the right hand of the needy raises him up.

hard.q: How can a psalm in the Bible pray for an enemy's children to be orphaned and beggars?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest texts in the Psalter, and Christians have answered it in several ways. Some read verses 6 to 19 as the enemies' curse against the psalmist, quoted and then refuted; on that reading the worst words are not the psalmist's at all. Others take them as his own and point out that he hands vengeance to God rather than acting on it, that the curses match the law's penalty for false witness, and that the enemy had hounded the poor to death. On this view the psalm is a prayer for justice from a victim, and it is honest about the anger that injustice produces. Some interpreters add that these prayers belong to an older stage of revelation, and that Jesus' command to love enemies and bless those who curse calls believers beyond them, while others argue that the prayer for God to judge evil is never cancelled, only placed in God's hands and tempered by hope for the enemy's repentance. Most agree that the psalm is not a model for personal revenge; it is a place to bring rage before God instead of acting on it.

questions: The psalmist hands his desire for justice to God instead of taking revenge. What wrong done to you or to someone you love do you need to hand over to God in the same way?
The enemy's sin is that he “never thought to show kindness” and crushed the poor. Where does this psalm's anger at cruelty to the vulnerable challenge your own indifference?
How do you hold together the honest anger of this psalm and Jesus' command to bless those who curse you?
